etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English delaien, borrowed from Anglo-Norman delaier, Old French deslaier, from des- + Old French laier (“to leave”), a conflation of Old Frankish *lattjan ("to delay, hinder"; from Proto-Germanic *latjaną (“to delay, hinder, stall”), from Proto-Indo-European *leh₁d- (“to leave, leave behind”)), and Old Frankish *laibijan ("to leave"; from Proto-Germanic *laibijaną (“to leave, cause to stay”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“to remain, continue”)). Doublet of dally.

Akin to Old English latian (“to delay, hesitate”), Old English latu (“a delay, a hindrance”), Old English lǣfan (“to leave”). More at let (to hinder), late, leave.

definitions.definition: A period of time before an event occurs; the act of delaying; procrastination; lingering inactivity.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Acts 25:17:
quote.text: Without any delay, on the morrow I sat on the judgment seat.

quote.citation: 1848, Thomas Babington Macaulay, The History of England from the Accession of James the Second, volume 1, London: A. and W. Galignani & Co., published 1849, page 522:
quote.text: The government ought to be settled without the delay of a day.

quote.citation: 2019 October, Ian Walmsley, “Cleaning up”, in Modern Railways, page 42:
quote.text: In this article I'm thinking about the big delays, over two hours. While rare, they make the news and help to deter people from future rail travel, both travellers and news viewers.

definitions.definition: (music) An audio effects unit that introduces a controlled delay.

quote.citation: 2014, Dave Hunter, Guitar Amps and Effects For Dummies, page 259:
quote.text: The 8-bit sound quality of many early delays did indeed leave a lot to be desired (compare this to the 16-bit digital technology of CDs)

definitions.definition: (programming, Clojure) Synonym of promise (“object representing delayed result”)
(chess) An amount of time provided on each move before one's clock starts to tick; a less common time control than increment.
(transitive, intransitive) To put off until a later time; to defer.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Matthew 24:48:

definitions.definition: To retard; to stop, detain, or hinder, for a time.

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter X, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: Mr. Cooke had had a sloop yacht built at Far Harbor, the completion of which had been delayed, and which was but just delivered.  […]  The Maria had a cabin, which was finished in hard wood and yellow plush, and accommodations for keeping things cold.

quote.citation: a. 1547, Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey, The faithful Lover declareth his Pains and his uncertain Joys, and with only Hope recomforteth somewhat his woful Heart:
quote.text: The watery showers delay the raging wind.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English delaien, from Old French delaiier, a variant of delaissier.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book III, Canto XII”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: Those dreadfull flames she also found delayd / And quenched quite like a consumed torch […].
